transcript.content: Hi, I'm Dr. Smith. Welcome in—what brings you here today?

I suppose I'm here because of work. I just... I can't seem to keep my mind on the actual experiments anymore. 

I'll be sitting in a grant call, or a safety meeting, and... I don't know, I'll notice a pump vibrating in the lab, or a student makes a side comment, or I'll remember some odd peak in an old spectrum. And suddenly I'm just... off chasing that for hours. While the thing everyone actually needs from me just falls apart.
Has this kind of difficulty staying focused and getting pulled into side details been something you've dealt with since you were a child, or is this a new pattern that's developed more recently?

No... not since childhood. Just recently. 

About seven months, I think. Right around when I took over the multi-site spectroscopy project.
Over these past seven months, have you also noticed times when your mood felt unusually elevated, irritable, or your energy was much higher than normal, along with needing less sleep than usual?

I don't really think of it as elevated. It's just... for months, it felt like the lab was finally moving at my speed. Electrified, almost. 

But... I suppose I have been irritable. If someone questions my plan, or tells me to slow down, I... I tend to snap at them. I'm pretty sure the students are avoiding my office now.
Before these past seven months, have you ever had earlier periods—lasting a week or more—where you felt unusually high-energy or elated, or conversely, deeply depressed and low?

I... I don't really know. 

I've always just been focused on my work. I don't keep track of my moods like that. It's just... work.
During these past seven months, have you noticed that you need less sleep than usual but still feel rested and full of energy?

Yes... I suppose. 

Most nights, I'm only getting maybe two or three hours. I usually just end up on the couch, laptop still open. 

But I'm not tired. I wake up sharp, and... ready to get back to work. Sleep just feels like an inefficient interruption right now. So I don't do much of it.
Have you ever had a period, at any point in your life, lasting two weeks or more, where you felt persistently sad, hopeless, or lost interest in things you used to enjoy?

No... I don't think so. 

I don't really dwell on things like that. If an experiment fails or funding falls through, I might get frustrated, but... not hopeless. I just move on to the next problem. I don't really have time to sit around feeling sad.

Thinking back to earlier chapters of your career or life—say, before you started this current position—was there ever a stretch of days or weeks where colleagues or family noticed you seeming unusually energetic, talkative, or driven, even if you didn't think much of it at the time?

I don't... I don't know. 

People don't really comment on my energy levels. We're all just focused on the research. If I was working hard, it was because the project needed it. I don't think anyone would have thought anything of it.
Over these past seven months, have you been using any substances, stimulants, or medications—like caffeine pills, energy drinks, or anything else—to help keep you going?

No. I don't use things like that. 

Just... regular coffee. Maybe a cup or two in the morning. That's all. I don't need anything else to keep going.
Over these past seven months, have you found yourself feeling unusually confident—like you have special insight, abilities, or importance that others don't fully recognize?

I wouldn't call it... unusual confidence. I just saw what needed fixing. 

The multi-site project was a mess, and... well, I knew I could rescue the whole thing by myself. I just had to redesign the spectroscopy approach. And I was stepping in to mentor the students, mostly because I could do it better than their actual advisors were. 

I would have beaten the grant deadline, too. I just... I really just needed people to stop getting in my way. That's all it was. Just knowing how to get the work done.

Doctor: Have you noticed your thoughts racing during this time, or felt like you were jumping from one idea to another faster than usual?

Patient: I... no, not racing. 

I was just thinking about the project. There were a lot of pieces to it. I had to keep track of them all. That's just how the work is.
